newsitem.title: switzerland: FOCUS-Swiss banks thankful boycott plan scrapped.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swiss banks thankful boycott plan scrapped.

text.p: Swiss banks welcomed on Thursday plans by Jewish leaders to scrap calls for a world boycott of Switzerland's globally active financial institutions over a dispute about lost accounts left by victims of the Holocaust.
The association of Switzerland's over 400 banks also urged New York city and state to reconsider their proposals for punitive measures.

The bankers' group was reacting to a World Jewish Congress (WJC) statement in New York that plans for a boycott had been dropped after the three biggest Swiss banks pledged to open a Holocaust memorial fund with 100 million Swiss francs ($70 million).
"We welcome reports that international Jewish organisations plan to drop boycott plans," association spokeswoman Silvia Matile said.
"This opens the way to constructive cooperation in the interests of the issue," she told Reuters.
Switzerland's biggest bank also welcomed the news.
"It is gratifying when we can talk with each other again and the situation relaxes," Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) spokeswoman Gertrud Erismann said.

Swiss banks and Jewish critics had been at loggerheads for months and tension was mounting before the biggest three banks -- UBS, Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) -- bowed to demands for a financial gesture of goodwill.
Jewish groups accuse banks of hoarding millions of dollars in wealth left by Holocaust victims. The banks have agreed under pressure to look but say the result will be less than imagined.
"Naturally we hope the New York authorities draw the same conclusions as WJC vice-president Kalman Sultanik," Matile said.

Sultanik said earlier a February 14 meeting in New York of the World Jewish Restitution Organisation that was to have discussed a boycott will now be attended by Swiss and U.S. officials and be used to discuss ways of cooperating with Switzerland.
The New York City Council and State Assembly both plan hearings next week on whether to make business more difficult for Swiss banks.

Matile said she was pleased to see the WJC recognising the efforts made so far by banks and authorities to track down lost assets stashed in neutral Switzerland to hide it from the Nazis and left in limbo when the oweners were killed in the Holocaust.

Under pressure led by the WJC, the banks last May created a joint commission with Jewish groups and headed by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker empowered to lift bank secrecy and hunt for Holocuast accounts.
"We will continue in the future to contribute to finding good and acceptable solutions," Matile said.
The bank's announcement on Wednesday added to pressure on the Swiss government to contribute to a Holocaust memorial fund.
Government officials said they were working on a decision as quickly as possible.
But commentators across the political spectrum urged Berne to stop hesitating and declare how much it would give.

Thomas Borer, special ambassador in charge of coordinating Berne's response to Holocaust questions, told Reuters the government was already working at speed on guidelines for a fund it may later join and which will include the bank payment.
"We will be discussing the concept of this fund with all interested sides in the next few days and weeks, including Jewish groups," Borer said.

But he reiterated the cabinet's official line that it would only decide whether and how much to pay after a panel of international historians presented its first findings on Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre.
"It is not enough to want to 'decide before summer'," wrote the leading conservative daily, the Neue Zuercher Zeitung (NZZ), referring to the government's timing for a decision.
($ = 1.424 Swiss Francs)
